sysd-reliab-179.title: Cascading failure triggers: what sets off the domino effect
sysd-reliab-179.text: A service already susceptible to cascades needs only a nudge. Cascading failure triggers are the disturbances that start the domino effect. Tasks may die and reduce capacity. One cause is a Query of Death, an RPC whose contents trigger a failure in the process; others are cluster issues and assertion failures. Pushing a new binary or configuration to many tasks at once can start a cascade. Often no change is behind it: usage simply grew without an adjustment to capacity. Drains and turndowns can remove capacity or add latency by sending requests to a distant cluster. During a cascade, check recent changes and consider reverting them.

sysd-reliab-180.title: Cold caches and slow starts
sysd-reliab-180.text: When most requests are served from caches, an empty cache makes 100% of requests costly. Processes also respond more slowly just after starting, for example while setting up connections. A cache is cold when a new cluster is turned up, a cluster returns from maintenance with possibly stale contents, or a restarted task must refill it. A latency cache lets a service sustain its expected load with an empty cache, while a capacity cache does not. To cope, overprovision, reject requests when overloaded, and add load to a cluster slowly so a small request rate warms the cache first.

sysd-reliab-183.title: Load testing to failure: finding the breaking point
sysd-reliab-183.text: Past its limit, a fragile component crashes or errors heavily, while a better one rejects a few requests and survives. Load testing to failure shows which one you have. It pushes each component until it breaks, to learn its breaking point and how it behaves beyond it before an overload hits. Past its limit, a component should serve errors or degraded results without cutting the rate of successful requests. Test gradual and impulse load, since caching effects differ, and test how the component returns to nominal load. Test each component separately, and test large clients, for instance whether they use the randomized delays described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-079}}.

sysd-reliab-177.title: Queue management for overload: reject early, wait less
sysd-reliab-177.text: A queue ten times the thread count turns a 100-millisecond request into 1.1 seconds once the queue is full, mostly spent waiting. Most thread-per-request servers put a queue in front of a thread pool, and usually a full queue makes the server reject new requests. For fairly steady traffic, a queue small relative to the thread pool, such as 50% or less, makes the server reject early. Bursty load may do better with a queue sized from the threads in use, the processing time per request, and the size and frequency of bursts. Limiting queue length is also a form of load shedding.

sysd-reliab-182.title: Preventing server overload, in rough priority order
sysd-reliab-182.text:
Servers should protect themselves from overload, and the defenses stack up in rough priority order. First comes load testing the server's capacity limits and its failure mode for overload. It is the most important exercise, because without a realistic test it is hard to predict which resource will be exhausted and how. Next, serve lower-quality, cheaper-to-compute results to the user, a strategy that is service-specific. Higher-level systems can reject requests instead of overloading servers. They can rate limit at reverse proxies by criteria such as IP address, at load balancers when the service enters global overload, and at individual tasks. Whatever the layer, an overloaded server should fail early and cheaply.

Good capacity planning, coupled with performance testing to find the load at which the service fails, reduces the chance of a cascade. For a 5,000 QPS breaking point and a 19,000 QPS peak, about six clusters give N + 2, a margin explained in {{ref:sysd-reliab-218}}. But planning is not sufficient. Losing major infrastructure, load balancing problems, partitions or unexpected traffic can create pockets of load beyond what was planned.

sysd-reliab-069.title: Retry strategies: how long to wait before trying again
sysd-reliab-069.text: Retrying is easy. Choosing how long to wait is the hard part. Retry strategies set that wait after a transient error, so network instability is handled without overloading the service. Linear backoff waits a progressively increasing fixed interval, which under high load or high concurrency can cause resource contention or retry storms. A faster-growing alternative grows the delay exponentially, for example 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds up to a maximum; see {{ref:sysd-reliab-079}}. It cuts load but can delay a fix that a quick retry would have achieved. Adding jitter, a random amount, to either one spreads retries over time, though large jitter can delay more than necessary.

sysd-reliab-067.title: Circuit breaker: stop calling a service that is failing
sysd-reliab-067.text:
A remote call, unlike an in-memory call, can fail or hang until a timeout. Many callers stuck on an unresponsive supplier can exhaust critical resources and cause failures that cascade across systems. A circuit breaker is a design pattern that wraps calls to a remote service, watches for failures and stops making the calls once failures pass a threshold.

The protected call is wrapped in a circuit breaker object. Once failures reach a threshold, the breaker trips, and all further calls return an error without the protected call being made. Timeout-only methods delay error responses or fail healthy requests prematurely. A circuit breaker instead detects unresponsive services dynamically and prevents repeated attempts.

It has a catch. Marc Brooker warns that circuit breakers can read a partial failure as total failure and bring down the whole system. Sharded and cell-based systems are especially vulnerable. One workaround is for the server to say which part is overloaded, so the client uses a matching mini circuit breaker, but that is complex and expensive.

sysd-reliab-071.title: Idempotency: making a repeated request safe
sysd-reliab-071.text:
After a payment request times out, the client cannot tell whether the server missed it, processed it and lost the response, or is still processing it. Retrying without idempotency can charge the customer twice. An operation is idempotent if applying it several times has the same effect as applying it once.

Setting a user's email to a@example.com is idempotent. 'Add $10 to the balance' is not, because every repeat changes the result. Looking up a customer, changing an address and canceling an order are idempotent, but placing an order is not, since multiple requests place multiple orders. HTTP standards say GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent and POST need not be; see {{ref:sysd-found-036}}. Idempotent means the same server state after one call or many, not an identical response, so a repeated DELETE may return 404.

The need is constant. Networks drop responses, clients time out and load balancers retry, so the same request often reaches a server more than once. Message brokers mostly offer at-least-once delivery, so consumers see duplicates, and double-clicks or page refreshes can duplicate submissions. With idempotency, an operation can be retried as often as necessary without unintended effects, so reliable systems can run on unreliable networks and clients can retry aggressively. Without it, the server must track whether an operation already ran. It is not free: it needs extra storage and lookups for keys, and extra logic for concurrent and in-flight requests.

sysd-reliab-079.title: Exponential backoff: waiting twice as long each time
sysd-reliab-079.text:
A mobile app that fails to connect tries again 1 second later, then 2 seconds, then 4. Each time, the pause is multiplied by a fixed amount, here 2. This is exponential backoff, an algorithm that uses feedback to multiplicatively decrease the rate of a process, to gradually find an acceptable rate. The delay is an exponential function of the number of adverse events observed.

It is a closed-loop control. It reduces the rate in response to adverse events such as a collision, packet loss, an error response from a service or an explicit request to back off. In rate limiting, each time a service says a client sends too often, the client cuts its rate by a predetermined factor until it reaches an acceptable equilibrium. Unlike a fixed limit, backoff works without giving the client prior information. Under heavy load it automatically lowers request rates, keeping some availability instead of overloading the service. TCP uses it too: when a segment's timer expires, the new timeout is twice the previous value.

sysd-reliab-175.title: Retry budgets: capping the retries that cause outages
sysd-reliab-175.text:
A backend limited to 10,000 QPS that receives 10,100 QPS rejects 100 requests. Their retries push it to 10,200 QPS, and growing retry volume can make it melt down and crash. A retry budget limits retries per request, per client or per server so retries cannot amplify an overload into a cascading failure.

A per-request budget of up to three attempts lets the failure bubble up after that. A request that hit overloaded tasks three times is unlikely to succeed when the whole datacenter is probably overloaded. A per-client budget tracks the ratio of requests that are retries and retries only while it is below 10%. That cuts worst-case request growth from just below 3X to 1.1x.

Layers multiply retries. If the backend, frontend and JavaScript layers each issue 3 retries, which is 4 attempts, one user action can create 64 attempts on the database. So retry only at the layer immediately above the one rejecting, never retry permanent errors, and always use randomized exponential backoff.

sysd-reliab-070.title: Exactly-once execution: retry plus a duplicate check
sysd-reliab-070.text:
A payment system must execute each payment order exactly once, because double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems a payment system can have. An operation is executed exactly once when it runs at least once and at most once at the same time. That looks hard, but it becomes easier when split in two: at-least-once is implemented with retry, and at-most-once with an idempotency check.

Retry provides the at-least-once guarantee. A client retries a payment after a network error or timeout, and it may only succeed at a later attempt. The idempotency check uses an idempotency key, usually a client-generated UUID that expires after a period. It is sent in an HTTP header such as idempotency-key so the server can discard duplicate payment requests.

Strictly, exactly-once processing is generally not achievable across a network. But at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing gives the same observable result, called effectively-once processing.

sysd-reliab-073.title: Idempotency keys: how a server spots a repeated request
sysd-reliab-073.text:
Some operations, such as POST /payments, are not naturally idempotent. For those, the client generates a unique key, usually a UUID, and sends it with the request, for example in an Idempotency-Key header. That idempotency key lets the server detect duplicates.

The server looks up the key. If it is absent, the server stores the key, processes the request and saves the response against the key. If it is present, the server skips processing and returns the saved response. Checking for the key and recording it must be atomic, or two concurrent retries can both pass the check. A database unique constraint or a Redis SET NX can do this.

The server should store a hash of the request payload and reject a repeated key that arrives with a different payload. A retry can also arrive while the original is still processing, and the server can return a 409 Conflict or make the retry wait. A retention period of a few hours to a few days is common and keeps storage cost bounded.

sysd-reliab-068.title: Circuit breaker states: closed, open and half-open
sysd-reliab-068.text: A circuit breaker is always in one of three states: closed, open or half-open. When everything is normal, it stays closed and all requests pass through. If failures rise beyond the threshold, it trips into the open state and returns an error immediately without invoking the service. After a timeout period, usually specified by the system watching the service, it moves to half-open. In the half-open state a limited number of requests pass through. If they succeed, the breaker returns to closed, and if they keep failing, it goes back to open. An alert is usually wanted whenever the breaker trips.

sysd-reliab-081.title: Backoff jitter: breaking up synchronized retries
sysd-reliab-081.text: If every sender backs off the same amount of time, every sender retransmits together and collides again, so a deterministic backoff is unsuitable for shared channels. Jitter adds randomness to the delays, so senders that fail together do not retry at the same moment. The exponential algorithm sets the range of possible delays, in slot times, a fixed unit of waiting. After the first collision the delay is 0 or 1, after the second 0 to 3, after the third 0 to 7. A wider range lowers the probability of a collision but increases the average latency. In retry strategies, jitter can be additive or multiplicative.

sysd-reliab-080.title: Truncated exponential backoff: putting a ceiling on the wait
sysd-reliab-080.text: Without a limit, an exponential delay can become undesirably long. Truncated exponential backoff caps the number of increases, so after a certain number the delay stops growing. This reduces unexpectedly long latencies and improves recovery times after a transient outage. In IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD the ceiling is 10, so the maximum delay is 1023 slot times. Choosing the limit balances collision probability against latency. A higher ceiling cuts collisions exponentially, but it widens the range of possible latencies and raises the average latency.

sysd-reliab-072.title: Where idempotency matters: payments, orders and accounts
sysd-reliab-072.text: Idempotency is essential wherever an operation might be retried or executed multiple times. In RESTful APIs, retrying must not execute the same operation several times, so idempotent methods such as PUT and DELETE keep resource states consistent. In payment processing, retries and network issues must not charge a customer several times. In order management, submitting an order several times must place one order and not deduct inventory twice. In account management, a retried registration must not create multiple accounts, and several password reset requests must result in a single reset. A reapplied database transaction must not change the state again, and handlers must tolerate repeated queue messages.

sysd-reliab-089.title: Hierarchical token bucket: sharing a link fairly
sysd-reliab-089.text: Shaping traffic only helps at the bottleneck between the LAN and the Internet, typically a home or office LAN served by a DSL or T1 connection. The hierarchical token bucket is an arrangement of token buckets in a hierarchy that limits each client's rate so that no client saturates the total bandwidth. It is a faster replacement for the class-based queueing discipline in Linux. Each class is given a rate, its guaranteed bandwidth, and a ceil, the maximum bandwidth it may consume. A class that requests more than its guaranteed bandwidth may borrow from its parent as long as both ceils are not reached.

sysd-reliab-074.title: Idempotent consumers: handling the same message twice
sysd-reliab-074.text: Message brokers usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, so a consumer must expect duplicates. An idempotent consumer handles a message that arrives more than once so that the repeat has no extra effect. A deduplication table stores the ID of each processed message and skips a message whose ID is already present. The ID is written in the same transaction as the side effect. Natural idempotency designs the operation so repeating it is harmless, for example 'set status to shipped' instead of 'advance status'. Versioning attaches a version or sequence number to updates and ignores any update that is not newer than the current state.

sysd-reliab-087.title: Traffic shaping and policing: delay it or drop it
sysd-reliab-087.text: Two ways of enforcing a traffic limit treat the excess differently. In traffic policing, packets that do not conform to the limits may be dropped or reduced in priority, for downstream traffic management to drop if there is congestion. In traffic shaping, packets are delayed until they conform. Both are commonly used to protect the network against excess or excessively bursty traffic. Hosts commonly shape traffic at their network interfaces so that their transmissions are not discarded by traffic management functions in the network.

sysd-reliab-090.title: Token bucket versus leaky bucket: one algorithm, two names
sysd-reliab-090.text: Two algorithms with different names are, fundamentally, the same one. The token bucket is the mirror image of the leaky bucket as a meter. Conforming packets add fluid to a finite bucket that drains at a constant rate, matching tokens removed and added at a fixed rate. Implemented correctly with the same parameters, the two see exactly the same packets as conforming and nonconforming. The leaky bucket as a queue is different. It is a special case of the meter version, applies only to traffic shaping and gives jitter-free output. Both versions go by the same name in the literature, which has caused considerable confusion.

reviews.resilience-circuit-breakers-rate-limitin: The largest incidents begin small, and a cascading failure grows by positive feedback as overloaded parts push their work onto the rest. Fault tolerance keeps a service running through faults, and rate limiting, load shedding, deadlines and quotas keep any one server from being asked for too much. The token bucket, the leaky bucket and the window algorithms count the traffic behind those limits. Retries repair transient errors only when backoff, jitter and budgets bound them, and a circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service altogether. Idempotency, with its keys and idempotent consumers, makes a repeated request safe, and that is what lets a client retry aggressively.
